lessons.title: The Particle Model and Density
lessons.description: Atomic structure, particle model of matter, density calculations and measurement.
lessons.content_html:
Atomic Structure and the Particle Model

Everything around you is made of atoms. An atom has a tiny, positively charged nucleus at its centre, made up of protons and neutrons. Negatively charged electrons orbit the nucleus at different distances. The nuclear radius is much smaller than the overall radius of the atom, and almost all of the atom’s mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

A typical atom has a radius of about \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m. The nucleus is roughly 10,000 times smaller than the atom itself, meaning atoms are mostly empty space. To put this in perspective, if an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be no bigger than a marble sitting at the centre — yet that marble would contain virtually all of the atom’s mass.

Inside the nucleus, protons carry a positive charge and neutrons carry no charge. The number of protons defines which element the atom belongs to (its atomic number). In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the overall charge is zero. If an atom gains or loses electrons it becomes a charged particle called an ion.

Key Fact

The atom has a positively charged nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by negatively charged electrons. The nuclear radius is much smaller than the atomic radius, and almost all the mass is in the nucleus.

How the Atomic Model Changed Over Time

Our understanding of the atom developed through key scientific discoveries. Each new model replaced the last when experimental evidence showed the old model could not explain what scientists observed. This is a powerful example of how the scientific method works — models are updated or replaced as new evidence emerges.

Thomson’s Model (1897): J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the “plum pudding” model — a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a pudding. This was the first model to include subatomic particles.

Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden (1909): The alpha particle scattering experiment fired positively charged alpha particles at a thin sheet of gold foil. Most alpha particles passed straight through, showing the atom is mostly empty space. However, a small number were deflected at large angles, and a few bounced straight back. This could only be explained by a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre of the atom. The plum pudding model was abandoned.

Bohr’s Model (1913): Niels Bohr refined the nuclear model by suggesting electrons orbit the nucleus at specific, fixed energy levels (shells), rather than randomly. Electrons can only exist in these allowed orbits, and they jump between energy levels by absorbing or emitting specific amounts of energy. This explained the emission spectra of elements — the distinct colours of light produced when elements are heated.

Modern model: Later work showed that electrons do not follow neat circular orbits. Instead, they exist in “clouds” of probability around the nucleus. For GCSE, the Bohr model with its electron shells is the version you need to use and understand.

Particle Arrangements in the Three States of Matter

The particle model explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases based on how their particles are arranged and how they move. Although the particles are far too small to see directly, the model successfully predicts observable properties like shape, volume and compressibility.

In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction. They vibrate about these positions but cannot move from place to place. This is why solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume. The regular arrangement of particles in many solids forms a lattice structure.

In a liquid, particles are close together but can slide past each other because the forces between them are weaker than in a solid. Liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container. In a gas, particles are far apart with negligible forces between them. They move rapidly in random directions, colliding with each other and the walls of their container. Gases fill any container they are placed in and can be compressed because of the large spaces between particles.

What Is Density?

Density tells you how much mass is packed into a given volume. A dense material has a lot of mass in a small volume. The equation is:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

Where \(\rho\) is density (\(\text{kg/m}^3\)), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(V\) is volume (\(\text{m}^3\)). You may also see density expressed in \(\text{g/cm}^3\). To convert, remember that \(1 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3\). You must be able to rearrange this equation to find mass (\(m = \rho \times V\)) or volume (\(V = \frac{m}{\rho}\)).

Key Fact

Density = mass ÷ volume. Solids generally have higher densities than liquids because their particles are more closely packed. Gases have much lower densities because particles are spread far apart.

Question: A metal block has a mass of 540 g and a volume of \(200 \text{ cm}^3\). Calculate its density in \(\text{g/cm}^3\).

Answer: Write the equation: \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\). Substitute: \(\rho = \frac{540}{200} = 2.7 \text{ g/cm}^3\). This matches the density of aluminium. To express in SI units: \(2.7 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 2700 \text{ kg/m}^3\).

Investigating Density (PAG P1)

To measure the density of a regular solid (such as a cuboid), measure its mass on a balance and calculate its volume using a ruler: \(V = \text{length} \times \text{width} \times \text{height}\). For a cylinder, use \(V = \pi r^2 h\).

For an irregular solid (like a pebble), use a eureka (displacement) can. Fill the can until water is level with the spout. Gently lower the object into the water and collect the displaced water in a measuring cylinder. The volume of displaced water equals the volume of the object. Alternatively, use a measuring cylinder directly: record the initial water level, submerge the object, and read the new level. The difference is the object’s volume.

For a liquid, measure the mass of an empty measuring cylinder on a balance. Pour in the liquid and measure the total mass. The liquid’s mass equals the difference between the two readings. Read the volume from the measuring cylinder scale at the bottom of the meniscus, then apply \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\).

In solids, particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement, giving high density. In liquids, particles are still close but less ordered, so density is slightly lower. In gases, particles are far apart with large gaps, so density is much lower — typically about 1000 times less than solids.

Crucially, mass is conserved during a change of state. When ice melts to water, the same number of particles is present but they occupy a slightly different volume. When water boils to steam, the mass stays the same but the volume increases enormously, so the density drops dramatically. An unusual exception is water itself: ice is slightly less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats.

Common sources of error include: reading the measuring cylinder at an angle (parallax error), not drying the object before measuring its mass, and air bubbles clinging to the surface of an irregular solid during displacement. To improve accuracy, take repeat measurements and calculate a mean, use a balance with higher resolution, and ensure the object is fully submerged.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In OCR Gateway Physics, density calculation questions are common. Always write the equation first, substitute the values with correct units, and show your working. If asked to describe an experiment to measure density, name the equipment (balance, ruler or eureka can, measuring cylinder) and describe the method step by step. Remember to convert units if needed — \(1 \text{ m}^3 = 1{,}000{,}000 \text{ cm}^3\) and \(1 \text{ g/cm}^3 = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3\).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atoms have a small, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons. The atomic model developed from Thomson’s plum pudding, through Rutherford’s nuclear model, to Bohr’s electron shells.
  • The particle model explains solids (fixed, vibrating in a lattice), liquids (close, sliding past each other) and gases (far apart, rapid random motion).
  • Density \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\). You must be able to calculate density, rearrange the equation, and describe experiments to measure it for regular solids, irregular solids and liquids.

lessons.title: Changes of State and Internal Energy
lessons.description: Specific heat capacity, specific latent heat, and gas pressure at constant volume.
lessons.content_html:
Changes of State

Matter can change between three states — solid, liquid and gas. These are physical changes: they can be reversed, and the original properties of the substance are recovered. Crucially, mass is conserved during any change of state — no atoms are created or destroyed, they simply rearrange.

The key changes of state are: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), evaporation/boiling (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), and sublimation (solid directly to gas, such as dry ice turning to carbon dioxide gas).

There is an important difference between evaporation and boiling. Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid at any temperature — the fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape as gas. Boiling occurs throughout the entire liquid at a specific, fixed temperature (the boiling point) when enough energy is supplied. Evaporation causes cooling because the most energetic particles leave, reducing the average kinetic energy of those left behind.

Key Fact

Mass is conserved during all changes of state. Physical changes differ from chemical changes because the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.

Internal Energy and Heating

When you heat a substance, you increase the internal energy of the system. Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy stored by all the particles. It is important to distinguish between temperature and internal energy: temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, while internal energy includes both kinetic and potential energy contributions.

Heating can do one of two things:

• Raise the temperature — particles move faster (or vibrate more vigorously), increasing their kinetic energy. The substance stays in the same state.
• Cause a change of state — particles gain potential energy to overcome the forces of attraction between them, but the temperature stays constant during the change. All the energy goes into breaking (or forming) intermolecular bonds.

A heating curve shows temperature on the y-axis against time (or energy supplied) on the x-axis. The curve has sloping sections (temperature rising, kinetic energy of particles increasing) and flat sections (temperature constant, change of state occurring as potential energy increases).

The first flat section is at the melting point (solid to liquid). The second flat section is at the boiling point (liquid to gas). During these plateaus, the substance is a mixture of two states. The length of each flat section depends on the specific latent heat of the substance — a longer flat section means more energy is needed for that change of state.

The gradient of the sloping sections depends on the specific heat capacity: a material with a high SHC will have a gentler slope because it takes more energy per degree of temperature rise.

Specific Heat Capacity

Specific heat capacity (SHC) tells you how much energy is needed to heat up a material. Different materials require different amounts of energy for the same temperature rise. Water has a high SHC of 4200 J/kg °C, meaning it takes a lot of energy to heat — this is why water is used in central heating systems and why coastal areas have milder climates.

The equation linking energy change to temperature change is:

$$\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta \theta$$

Where \(\Delta E\) is the change in thermal energy (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), \(c\) is the specific heat capacity (J/kg °C), and \(\Delta \theta\) is the change in temperature (°C). You must be able to rearrange this equation — for example, to find the temperature change: \(\Delta \theta = \frac{\Delta E}{m \times c}\).

Question: How much energy is needed to heat 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C? (SHC of water = 4200 J/kg °C)

Answer: \(\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta \theta = 2 \times 4200 \times (100 - 20) = 2 \times 4200 \times 80 = 672{,}000 \text{ J} = 672 \text{ kJ}\)

To investigate the SHC of a metal block: drill two holes in the block — one for a thermometer and one for an electrical heater. Measure the block's mass on a balance. Record the starting temperature, turn on the heater, and record the energy supplied (using a joulemeter) and the final temperature. Calculate \(c = \frac{\Delta E}{m \times \Delta \theta}\). The main source of error is heat loss to the surroundings — insulating the block with a lagging jacket reduces this.

Specific Latent Heat

Specific latent heat (SLH) is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance at constant temperature. There are two types:

• Specific latent heat of fusion (\(L_f\)) — energy to change 1 kg from solid to liquid at the melting point. For water, \(L_f = 334{,}000 \text{ J/kg}\).
• Specific latent heat of vaporisation (\(L_v\)) — energy to change 1 kg from liquid to gas at the boiling point. For water, \(L_v = 2{,}260{,}000 \text{ J/kg}\).

The latent heat of vaporisation is always much larger than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance, because the particles must completely overcome the intermolecular forces to become a gas. The equation is:

$$E = m \times L$$

Where \(E\) is the thermal energy for a change of state (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(L\) is the specific latent heat (J/kg).

Key Fact

During a change of state, energy is transferred but the temperature does not change. This energy goes into breaking or forming bonds between particles (changing potential energy), not increasing kinetic energy.

Gas Pressure and Temperature

In a gas, particles are constantly moving and colliding with the walls of their container, creating pressure. Each collision exerts a tiny force on the wall. The total of all these collisions across the entire wall produces the overall gas pressure.

If you heat a gas at constant volume, the particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. This has two effects: collisions with the walls become more frequent and each collision is more forceful. Both factors increase the gas pressure. This is a qualitative relationship only at GCSE — you need to explain the trend, not calculate pressure values.

This has real-world safety implications. Sealed containers (such as aerosol cans or gas cylinders) can be dangerous if heated, because the increasing pressure may exceed the strength of the container, causing it to explode. This is why aerosol cans carry warnings not to expose them to temperatures above 50 °C.
lessons.exam_tip_html: OCR Gateway frequently tests the SHC and SLH equations. Always start by writing the correct equation, then substitute values clearly. Watch out for whether the question asks about temperature change (use \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)) or change of state (use \(E = mL\)). Remember: during a change of state, temperature stays constant even though energy is being supplied. If a question combines both (e.g. heating ice from -10 °C to steam at 100 °C), you need to break the calculation into separate stages.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mass is conserved during all changes of state. Physical changes are reversible; the original properties are recovered. Evaporation occurs at the surface at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.
  • Use \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\) for temperature changes and \(E = mL\) for changes of state. During a change of state, temperature remains constant as energy goes into overcoming intermolecular forces.
  • Increasing the temperature of a gas at constant volume increases its pressure because particles move faster, collide more frequently, and hit the walls with greater force.

lessons.title: Motion
lessons.description: Speed, velocity, acceleration, distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
lessons.content_html:
Speed and Velocity

Speed tells you how fast an object is moving. It is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction. The equation linking distance, speed and time is:

$$s = v \times t$$

Where \(s\) is distance (m), \(v\) is speed (m/s), and \(t\) is time (s). You can rearrange this to find speed (\(v = \frac{s}{t}\)) or time (\(t = \frac{s}{v}\)). Typical speeds to know include: walking (~1.5 m/s), running (~3 m/s), cycling (~6 m/s), a car in town (~13 m/s or 30 mph), and the speed of sound in air (~340 m/s).

Velocity is speed in a stated direction. It is a vector quantity. An object travelling in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because its direction constantly changes — meaning it is always accelerating, even though its speed stays the same.

Similarly, distance (scalar) measures total ground covered, while displacement (vector) measures how far and in what direction from the start. A runner who completes a 400 m lap of a track covers a distance of 400 m but has a displacement of zero — they end up back where they started.

Key Fact

Speed and distance are scalars (magnitude only). Velocity and displacement are vectors (magnitude + direction). An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity.

Acceleration

Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. An object accelerates when it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

Where \(a\) is acceleration (\(\text{m/s}^2\)), \(v\) is final velocity (m/s), \(u\) is initial velocity (m/s), and \(t\) is time (s). A negative value of acceleration means the object is decelerating (slowing down). For example, a car braking from 20 m/s to 0 m/s in 5 s has an acceleration of \(a = \frac{0 - 20}{5} = -4 \text{ m/s}^2\).

For uniform (constant) acceleration, you also need the equation:

$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

Where \(s\) is distance (m). This is useful when time is not given in the question. It is particularly important for braking distance calculations.

Question: A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 10 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.

Answer: \(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{25 - 5}{10} = \frac{20}{10} = 2 \text{ m/s}^2\)

Distance-Time Graphs

On a distance-time graph, the gradient (slope) of the line equals the speed. You can interpret the shape of the line as follows:

• A horizontal line means the object is stationary (speed = 0).
• A straight diagonal line means constant speed — the steeper the gradient, the faster the speed.
• A curve getting steeper means the object is accelerating.
• A curve getting shallower means the object is decelerating.

To find the speed at a specific instant on a curved d-t graph, draw a tangent to the curve at that point and calculate the gradient of the tangent.

Velocity-Time Graphs

On a velocity-time graph, two key pieces of information can be extracted:

• The gradient equals the acceleration. A steeper slope means greater acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity (zero acceleration). A downward slope means deceleration.
• A line below the x-axis means the object is moving in the opposite direction.

The area under the line on a velocity-time graph equals the distance travelled. For a triangle, the area is \(\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}\). For a rectangle, it is \(\text{base} \times \text{height}\). For irregular shapes, split the area into triangles and rectangles and add them together.

Key Fact

On a distance-time graph, gradient = speed. On a velocity-time graph, gradient = acceleration.

Key Fact

On a velocity-time graph, the area under the line = distance travelled. Split complex shapes into triangles and rectangles to calculate the total area.

Any moving object has kinetic energy. The equation is:

$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2$$

Where \(E_k\) is kinetic energy (J), \(m\) is mass (kg) and \(v\) is speed (m/s). Because speed is squared, doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy. This has critical implications for braking distances and road safety: a car travelling at 40 mph has four times the kinetic energy of one at 20 mph, meaning it needs four times the braking distance to stop.

Average Speed and Non-Uniform Motion

Most real journeys involve varying speeds. When an object's speed varies, you calculate average speed by dividing the total distance by the total time:

$$\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$$

On a distance-time graph with a curved line, you can estimate speed at a particular moment by drawing a tangent and finding its gradient. The average speed between two points is found by drawing a straight line (chord) between them and calculating its gradient.

To measure the speed of a trolley rolling down a ramp, mark a measured distance on the ramp with two markers. Use a stopwatch to time how long the trolley takes to travel between them, then calculate speed using \(v = \frac{s}{t}\). For greater precision, use light gates connected to a data logger — these measure very short time intervals as the trolley passes through, allowing you to calculate instantaneous speed. To investigate acceleration, use two light gates at different positions and compare the speeds.

For velocity-time graphs, calculate acceleration from the gradient and distance from the area under the line. Always show your working: identify the values you’re reading from the graph, write the formula, substitute, and include units in your answer. Remember to draw tangents on curved graphs to find instantaneous values.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Speed is scalar; velocity is a vector (speed + direction). Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time.
  • On d-t graphs: gradient = speed (draw tangent for curves). On v-t graphs: gradient = acceleration, area under = distance.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws
lessons.description: Newton's three laws of motion, resultant forces, momentum and inertia.
lessons.content_html:
Newton’s First Law

Newton’s First Law states that an object remains at rest or continues to move at a constant velocity unless acted upon by a resultant force. This means:

• If the resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays still and a moving object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
• If there is a resultant force, the object accelerates — which means it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction.

This law applies to all objects, from cars on motorways to planets orbiting the Sun. A book on a table remains stationary because its weight (downward) is exactly balanced by the normal contact force from the table (upward). A spacecraft drifting in deep space, where there is no friction or air resistance, will continue at the same velocity forever unless a thruster fires.

Key Fact

Objects do not need a force to keep moving at constant velocity. A resultant force is only needed to change the speed or direction of an object.

Newton’s Second Law: F = ma

Newton’s Second Law tells us that the resultant force on an object is equal to its mass multiplied by its acceleration:

$$F = m \times a$$

Where \(F\) is force in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration in \(\text{m/s}^2\). This equation tells you two important things: a bigger force produces a bigger acceleration (if mass stays the same), and a heavier object needs a bigger force for the same acceleration. It can be rearranged to find acceleration (\(a = \frac{F}{m}\)) or mass (\(m = \frac{F}{a}\)).

Remember that \(F\) in this equation is always the resultant force, not just any single force. If a car’s engine provides 3000 N of driving force but friction and air resistance total 1000 N, the resultant force is \(3000 - 1000 = 2000 \text{ N}\) forward.

Question: A 1500 kg car experiences a resultant force of 4500 N. Calculate its acceleration.

Answer: \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{4500}{1500} = 3 \text{ m/s}^2\)

You can investigate Newton’s Second Law using a trolley on a smooth track. Attach a string over a pulley to a hanging mass, which provides the force. Use light gates to measure the acceleration of the trolley. Keep the total mass of the system constant (trolley + hanging mass) and vary the force by moving masses from the trolley to the hanger. Plot a graph of force against acceleration — a straight line through the origin confirms that \(F \propto a\) at constant mass.

Weight, Mass and Gravitational Field Strength

Mass is the amount of matter in an object and is measured in kg. It does not change with location. Weight is the force of gravity acting on that mass, measured in newtons. The equation is:

$$W = m \times g$$

Where \(W\) is weight (N), \(m\) is mass (kg) and \(g\) is gravitational field strength (N/kg). On Earth, \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\). On the Moon, \(g \approx 1.6 \text{ N/kg}\), so a 70 kg person would weigh 700 N on Earth but only 112 N on the Moon. Their mass remains 70 kg in both locations. Weight is measured using a newton meter (spring balance), while mass is measured on a balance.

The numerical value of \(g\) at the Earth’s surface also equals the acceleration due to gravity in free fall: \(g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2\). This means that a falling object (ignoring air resistance) accelerates at \(10 \text{ m/s}^2\) regardless of its mass.

Newton’s Third Law

Newton’s Third Law states: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. These action-reaction pairs act on different objects and are always the same type of force. For example:

• When you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you with an equal force (both are normal contact forces).
• When the Earth pulls you down by gravity (your weight), you pull the Earth up with the same gravitational force.
• A swimmer pushes water backwards; the water pushes the swimmer forwards.

A common mistake is to identify weight and normal contact force as a Third Law pair. They are not — both act on the same object (you). A true Third Law pair involves forces on different objects.

Key Fact

Newton’s Third Law pairs are equal in size, opposite in direction, the same type of force, and act on different objects.

Terminal Velocity

When a skydiver jumps from a plane, they initially accelerate because their weight is much greater than air resistance. As speed increases, air resistance increases (it depends on speed, surface area and shape). Eventually, air resistance equals weight. At this point the resultant force is zero and the skydiver reaches terminal velocity — constant speed, zero acceleration.

When the parachute opens, the surface area dramatically increases, causing air resistance to suddenly become much greater than weight. The skydiver decelerates. As they slow down, air resistance decreases until a new, lower terminal velocity is reached — slow enough for a safe landing.

Momentum is a measure of how hard it is to stop a moving object. The equation is:

$$p = m \times v$$

Where \(p\) is momentum (kg m/s), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(v\) is velocity (m/s). In a closed system (where no external forces act), the total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after — this is the conservation of momentum. For example, if two trolleys of equal mass collide and stick together, their combined speed will be half of the original speed of the moving trolley.

Inertia is a measure of how difficult it is to change an object’s velocity. An object with more mass has more inertia. Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force to acceleration: \(m = \frac{F}{a}\). This is essentially Newton’s Second Law rearranged.
lessons.exam_tip_html: F = ma questions are very common in OCR Gateway. Always identify the resultant force first — you may need to subtract friction or air resistance. Show the equation, substitute values with units, and state the direction of acceleration if asked. For Newton’s Third Law, always name both forces, state they are equal and opposite, and emphasise they act on different objects.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • First Law: no resultant force = no change in motion. Second Law: \(F = ma\) (\(F\) is always the resultant force). Third Law: equal and opposite forces of the same type on different objects.
  • Weight \(W = mg\). On Earth, \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\). Mass is constant; weight varies with gravitational field strength. \(g\) also equals the acceleration in free fall.
  • Momentum \(p = mv\) is conserved in closed systems. Terminal velocity occurs when driving force = resistive force (resultant = 0).

lessons.title: Forces in Action
lessons.description: Hooke's law, elastic and plastic deformation, weight, gravity and gravitational PE.
lessons.content_html:
Stretching and Deformation

To stretch, bend or compress an object, more than one force must be applied. A single force would simply cause the object to accelerate (Newton's Second Law). Two opposing forces are needed for deformation — for example, a weight pulling a spring down while the support holds it up.

When forces are applied to a spring, it can undergo two types of deformation:

• Elastic deformation — the object returns to its original shape and size when the force is removed. The spring "bounces back."
• Plastic deformation — the object is permanently deformed and does not return to its original shape. The spring has been stretched beyond its limit.

Hooke's Law

Hooke's Law states that the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, as long as the elastic limit is not exceeded. The equation is:

$$F = k \times e$$

Where \(F\) is force (N), \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m), and \(e\) is extension (m). A larger spring constant means a stiffer spring that is harder to stretch. Extension means the change in length — so \(e = \text{stretched length} - \text{original length}\).

On a force-extension graph, the linear (proportional) region appears as a straight line through the origin. The gradient of this straight line equals the spring constant \(k\). Beyond the elastic limit, the graph curves upwards — this is the non-linear region where Hooke's Law no longer applies and the spring is undergoing plastic deformation.

Key Fact

Hooke's Law: \(F = ke\). The force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin up to the elastic limit. Beyond this, deformation becomes plastic (permanent).

Clamp a spring vertically from a stand. Measure and record the original length using a ruler. Add known masses one at a time, recording the new length each time. Calculate the extension for each mass (\(e = \text{new length} - \text{original length}\)). Plot force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis). The straight-line section confirms Hooke's Law. The point where the line begins to curve marks the elastic limit. To improve accuracy, take three readings at each force and calculate the mean, check for parallax by reading the ruler at eye level, and ensure the spring hangs freely without touching the stand.

When a spring is stretched, energy is stored as elastic potential energy. This can be calculated using:

$$E_e = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times e^2$$

Where \(E_e\) is elastic potential energy (J), \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m), and \(e\) is the extension (m). This equation only works within the elastic limit (the linear region). On a force-extension graph, the elastic potential energy equals the area under the straight-line section (which forms a triangle: \(\frac{1}{2} \times F \times e\)). When the spring is released, this stored energy is transferred to kinetic energy or other forms.

Gravity and Weight

All matter has a gravitational field that attracts other masses. Every object with mass creates a gravitational field around it, but the field is only noticeable for very massive objects like planets, moons and stars. The gravitational field strength at the Earth's surface is \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\), meaning every kilogram of mass experiences a gravitational force of 10 N.

Weight is the force of gravity on an object: \(W = m \times g\). It is measured using a newton meter (spring balance) and always acts downwards towards the centre of the Earth. The acceleration due to gravity in free fall equals \(g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2\) — numerically the same as gravitational field strength but with different units.

Gravitational Potential Energy

When an object is raised above the ground, work is done against gravity and energy is stored as gravitational potential energy (GPE):

$$E_p = m \times g \times h$$

Where \(E_p\) is GPE (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), \(g\) is gravitational field strength (N/kg), and \(h\) is height (m). If the object falls, this GPE is converted to kinetic energy (assuming no air resistance). At the top of a roller coaster, GPE is at its maximum; at the bottom, it has all been transferred to kinetic energy.

Work done equals the energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance. The equation is:

$$W = F \times d$$

Where \(W\) is work done (J), \(F\) is force (N), and \(d\) is distance along the line of action of the force (m). One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre. Work done and energy transferred are always equal — 1 J = 1 N m. The distance must be measured in the same direction as the force. If you carry a box horizontally, you do no work against gravity because the force (weight) acts downwards, perpendicular to your motion.

Key Fact

Work done \(W = Fd\) = energy transferred. Gravitational PE \(E_p = mgh\). Elastic PE \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\). All measured in joules (J).

Power

Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy:

$$P = \frac{W}{t}$$

Where \(P\) is power (W), \(W\) is work done or energy transferred (J), and \(t\) is time (s). One watt equals one joule per second. A 60 W light bulb transfers 60 J of energy every second. A more powerful engine can do the same amount of work in less time — or more work in the same time — compared to a less powerful one. For example, two students who both climb the same flight of stairs do the same work against gravity (\(W = mgh\)), but the student who climbs faster has a greater power output.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Hooke’s Law practical (PAG P2) is commonly examined. You should be able to describe the method, plot force against extension, identify the elastic limit on the graph, and calculate the spring constant from the gradient. Always use the equation \(F = ke\) for the linear section only. Remember that extension means the change in length, not the total length.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hooke’s Law: \(F = ke\) up to the elastic limit. Beyond this, deformation is plastic (permanent). Elastic PE = \(\frac{1}{2}ke^2\) (area under the F-e graph).
  • Weight \(W = mg\) (\(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\) on Earth). GPE \(E_p = mgh\). Work done \(W = Fd\). Power \(P = \frac{W}{t}\). All energy measured in joules.
  • Gravitational fields cause attraction between all masses. Stronger fields exist around more massive objects.

lessons.title: Static Charge and Simple Circuits
lessons.description: Electrostatics, charge flow, current, potential difference, resistance and Ohm's law.
lessons.content_html:
Static Electricity

Charge is a fundamental property of all matter. In most objects, the number of positive and negative charges is equal, so the object has zero net charge and appears electrically neutral. When two insulating materials are rubbed together, friction causes electrons to transfer from one surface to the other, creating static electricity.

The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses electrons becomes positively charged. It is always the electrons that move — protons are locked inside the nucleus and cannot transfer between objects. For example, when a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth, electrons move from the cloth to the rod: the rod becomes negative and the cloth becomes positive.

Static charge only builds up on insulators because electrons cannot flow away through the material. On a conductor, any excess charge would immediately spread out or flow to earth. If enough static charge builds up, it can discharge as a spark — this is what causes lightning, where charge jumps between clouds and the ground.

Key Fact

Static electricity is caused by the transfer of electrons between insulating materials. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. Only electrons move — protons stay in the nucleus.

Current, Charge and Time

Current is the rate of flow of charge through a conductor. In metals, it is free electrons that carry the charge. For current to flow, two conditions must be met: there must be a source of potential difference (voltage), and the circuit must be a closed loop with no gaps.

The equation linking charge, current and time is:

$$Q = I \times t$$

Where \(Q\) is charge (coulombs, C), \(I\) is current (amperes, A), and \(t\) is time (seconds, s). One ampere means one coulomb of charge passes a point in the circuit every second. In a single closed loop (series circuit), the current is the same at every point — charge is not used up as it flows through components.

Current is measured with an ammeter, connected in series. Potential difference is measured with a voltmeter, connected in parallel across the component being tested.

Resistance and Ohm’s Law

Resistance opposes the flow of current. The greater the resistance, the smaller the current for a given voltage. The relationship between potential difference, current and resistance is:

$$V = I \times R$$

Where \(V\) is potential difference (V), \(I\) is current (A), and \(R\) is resistance (\(\Omega\)). This can be rearranged to find current (\(I = \frac{V}{R}\)) or resistance (\(R = \frac{V}{I}\)). Strictly speaking, Ohm’s law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature remains constant. This only applies to ohmic conductors — components whose resistance does not change with current.

In a series circuit, all components are connected in a single loop. Current is the same everywhere. Potential difference is shared between components — the sum of voltages across all components equals the supply voltage. Total resistance = sum of individual resistances: \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\).

In a parallel circuit, components are on separate branches. Potential difference is the same across each branch. Current splits between branches — more current flows through the branch with lower resistance. Adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance because there are more paths for current to flow. This is why household circuits use parallel wiring: each appliance gets the full mains voltage, and one device failing does not break the others.

I-V Characteristics

An I-V characteristic graph shows how current varies with potential difference for a component. You should know the shapes for three key components:

• Resistor (ohmic conductor): a straight line through the origin. The gradient is constant, meaning resistance does not change. This confirms the component obeys Ohm’s law.
• Filament lamp: a curve that starts steep and flattens at higher voltages. As more current flows, the filament gets hotter, increasing its resistance. The curve is symmetrical in both directions (forward and reverse voltage).
• Diode: current only flows in one direction (the forward direction). In the reverse direction, resistance is so high that effectively no current flows. There is a threshold voltage (about 0.6 V for silicon) below which even forward current is negligible.

Key Fact

An ohmic conductor has a straight-line I-V graph (constant resistance). A filament lamp’s resistance increases with temperature (curved graph). A diode only conducts in one direction.

Some components have resistance that changes with environmental conditions:

• A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has high resistance in the dark and low resistance in bright light. It is used in circuits that need to respond to light levels, such as automatic streetlights and burglar alarms.
• An NTC thermistor (negative temperature coefficient) has high resistance when cold and low resistance when hot. It is used in temperature-sensing circuits such as thermostats, fire alarms, and car engine sensors.

Both LDRs and thermistors are used in potential divider circuits to produce a variable voltage output that depends on light or temperature.

For I-V characteristics, describe the shape of the graph and explain what it tells you about how resistance changes. Remember: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel.

  • Static electricity is caused by electron transfer between insulators. Like charges repel; opposites attract. Only electrons move.

lessons.title: Domestic Electricity and Electrical Power
lessons.description: AC and DC current, mains wiring safety, electrical power, energy transfer, and the National Grid transmission system.
lessons.content_html:
AC and DC

Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only — this is what batteries and solar cells produce. Alternating current (AC) constantly reverses direction, flowing back and forth through the circuit. The UK mains supply is AC at a frequency of 50 Hz (50 complete cycles per second) and a voltage of about 230 V.

On an oscilloscope trace, AC appears as a wave (typically a sine wave) that oscillates above and below zero. DC appears as a straight horizontal line. The key advantage of AC is that its voltage can be easily increased or decreased using transformers — this is essential for the efficient transmission of electricity through the National Grid.

Key Fact

The UK domestic supply is AC at 230 V and 50 Hz. Batteries supply DC. AC can be easily transformed to different voltages; DC cannot.

Mains Wiring and Safety

A UK three-pin plug contains three wires, each with a specific colour and function:

• Live (brown) — carries the AC supply at about 230 V. This wire is always dangerous, even when the switch is open, because it remains connected to the mains supply.
• Neutral (blue) — completes the circuit and is normally at 0 V. Current flows in through the live wire and out through the neutral.
• Earth (green and yellow striped) — a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. It provides a low-resistance path to earth if a fault occurs, preventing the casing from becoming live.

A fuse is always connected in the live wire. If the current exceeds the fuse rating, the thin fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, preventing overheating, fire or electrocution. The earth wire and fuse work together as a safety system: if the live wire touches the metal casing (a fault), a large current surges through the earth wire to ground, which immediately blows the fuse and disconnects the supply.

A residual current device (RCD) provides even faster protection. It compares the current in the live and neutral wires. If they differ (indicating current is leaking through a person or a fault), the RCD cuts the circuit within milliseconds.

The live wire alternates between approximately +325 V and -325 V (the 230 V rating is the root mean square value). Even when a switch is open (appliance turned off), the live wire is still connected to the mains supply and carries a potential of 230 V relative to earth. Touching it creates a large potential difference between your body and the ground, causing a dangerous current to flow through you. This is why you must never touch exposed wires or attempt to repair electrical appliances without disconnecting them from the mains.

Double insulation is an alternative safety feature used on appliances with plastic casings (such as hairdryers and power drills). The plastic casing cannot become live, so no earth wire is needed. These appliances are marked with a double-square symbol.

Electrical Power

Electrical power is the rate at which energy is transferred in a circuit. The key equations are:

$$P = V \times I$$

$$P = I^2 \times R$$

Where \(P\) is power (W), \(V\) is potential difference (V), \(I\) is current (A), and \(R\) is resistance (\(\Omega\)). The second equation is derived by substituting \(V = IR\) into the first. It is especially useful for calculating the power dissipated as heat in a resistor or in electrical cables.

Energy Transferred

The total energy transferred by an appliance depends on its power and how long it runs:

$$E = P \times t$$

Where \(E\) is energy (J), \(P\) is power (W) and \(t\) is time (s). Energy can also be calculated using charge: \(E = Q \times V\), where \(Q\) is charge (C) and \(V\) is potential difference (V). This tells you the energy transferred to each coulomb of charge as it passes through a component.

For domestic energy bills, energy is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) rather than joules. One kWh is the energy transferred by a 1 kW device running for 1 hour. To calculate the cost: \(\text{cost} = \text{energy (kWh)} \times \text{price per kWh}\). For example, a 3 kW oven running for 2 hours uses \(3 \times 2 = 6 \text{ kWh}\).

Key Fact

Power equations: \(P = VI\), \(P = I^2R\). Energy transferred: \(E = Pt\) or \(E = QV\). Domestic energy is measured in kWh. Cost = energy (kWh) × price per unit.

The National Grid

The National Grid is the nationwide system of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to consumers. Electricity is transmitted at very high voltages (up to 400,000 V) and correspondingly low currents to minimise energy losses in the cables.

The physics behind this is straightforward. Since \(P = V \times I\), transmitting the same power at higher voltage means a lower current. The power wasted as heat in the cables is \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 \times R\). Because current is squared, even a small reduction in current dramatically reduces heat losses. This is why the National Grid is efficient — only about 2% of energy is lost in transmission.

Step-up transformers at power stations increase the voltage (and reduce the current) for long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers at local substations reduce the voltage back to 230 V for safe domestic use.

For an ideal (100% efficient) transformer, the power input equals the power output:

$$V_p \times I_p = V_s \times I_s$$

Where \(V_p\) and \(I_p\) are the voltage and current in the primary coil, and \(V_s\) and \(I_s\) are those in the secondary coil. If voltage increases (step-up), current decreases proportionally — and vice versa for a step-down transformer. Transformers only work with AC because they rely on a changing magnetic field in the core to induce a voltage in the secondary coil.

For plug wiring, remember the colours: brown = live, blue = neutral, green/yellow = earth. The fuse always goes in the live wire. When choosing a fuse, pick the next standard rating above the normal operating current.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK mains: AC, 230 V, 50 Hz. Live (brown) is always dangerous, even when the switch is off. Fuse and earth wire protect against faults. RCDs provide faster protection.
  • Power: \(P = VI\), \(P = I^2R\). Energy: \(E = Pt\), \(E = QV\). Domestic energy in kWh. Cost = kWh × price per unit.
  • National Grid uses high voltage / low current to reduce \(I^2R\) energy losses in cables. Step-up and step-down transformers change voltage. Transformers only work with AC.

lessons.title: Magnets and Magnetic Fields
lessons.description: Permanent magnets, electromagnets, solenoids, Fleming's left-hand rule and motors.
lessons.content_html:
Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field at all times. It has a north pole and a south pole. The fundamental rule of magnetism is: like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Common permanent magnet materials include iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. These are called magnetic materials.

An induced magnet only becomes magnetic when placed inside a magnetic field. When the external field is removed, it loses its magnetism. An induced magnet is always attracted to the permanent magnet that magnetises it — never repelled — because the induced poles are always arranged so that unlike poles face each other. This is why a permanent magnet can pick up an iron nail, even though the nail is not itself a permanent magnet.

Key Fact

Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. A permanent magnet always has its own field. An induced magnet is temporary — it only has magnetism while in another magnet’s field.

Magnetic Fields

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a magnetic force acts on other magnetic materials or on moving charges. The field is represented by field lines, which show both the direction and the strength of the field:

• Field lines go from north to south outside the magnet (and from south to north inside).
• Where field lines are closer together, the field is stronger.
• The field is strongest at the poles and gets weaker further away.
• Field lines never cross each other.

You can map magnetic fields using a plotting compass: place the compass near the magnet, mark where the needle points, move the compass to the new position and repeat. Connect the dots to form smooth field lines from north to south. Iron filings sprinkled around a magnet provide a quick visual of the field pattern — they align along the field lines.

The Earth itself has a magnetic field, generated by convection currents in its liquid iron outer core. This is why a compass needle points towards geographic north (the Earth’s magnetic south pole is near the geographic north pole). The existence of the Earth’s magnetic field is evidence that the planet’s interior contains magnetic material.

When current flows through a straight wire, it creates a weak circular magnetic field around the wire. A solenoid is a wire wound into a coil — when current flows through it, the individual magnetic fields from each loop combine to produce a strong, uniform field inside the coil. The field pattern of a solenoid is very similar to that of a bar magnet, with a distinct north and south pole at each end.

Adding a soft iron core inside a solenoid creates an electromagnet. The iron core becomes an induced magnet and greatly strengthens the overall field. The strength of an electromagnet can be increased by: increasing the current, increasing the number of turns in the coil, and using a soft iron core. The key advantage over permanent magnets is that electromagnets can be switched on and off and their strength can be varied.

Applications of electromagnets include: scrapyard cranes (picking up and releasing metal), electric bells, relays, loudspeakers, and MRI scanners in hospitals.

The Motor Effect

When a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. This force arises because the magnetic field around the current-carrying wire interacts with the external magnetic field. The force is at its maximum when the wire is at right angles (perpendicular) to the field, and zero when the wire is parallel to the field.

The equation for the force on a conductor in a magnetic field is:

$$F = B \times I \times l$$

Where \(F\) is force (N), \(B\) is magnetic flux density (T, tesla), \(I\) is current (A), and \(l\) is the length of the conductor within the field (m). A stronger field, a larger current, or a longer wire all produce a greater force.

Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule

Fleming’s left-hand rule tells you the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field. Hold your left hand with thumb, first finger and second finger all at right angles to each other:

• Thumb = Force (motion/thrust)
• First finger = Field direction (north to south)
• Second finger = Current direction (conventional current, from positive to negative)

A useful mnemonic: thuMb = Motion, First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current. If any one of the three quantities reverses (e.g. the current direction reverses), the force reverses too.

Key Fact

Fleming’s LHR: Thumb = Force/Motion, First finger = Field (N to S), Second finger = Current (+ to -). The motor effect is the basis for how electric motors work.

In a simple DC electric motor, a current-carrying coil is placed in the magnetic field between two permanent magnets. Using Fleming’s left-hand rule, the two sides of the coil experience forces in opposite directions (because the current flows in opposite directions on each side). This pair of forces creates a turning effect (torque), causing the coil to rotate.

A split-ring commutator reverses the direction of current through the coil every half turn. Without this, the coil would rotate halfway and then stop. The commutator ensures the forces always push the coil in the same rotational direction, producing continuous spinning. The speed of the motor can be increased by using a stronger magnetic field, a larger current, or more turns on the coil.

If asked about electromagnets, explain how increasing current or turns strengthens the field. For the \(F = BIl\) equation, remember that \(B\) is magnetic flux density in tesla — a value will be given in the question. Show all working and units clearly. If the wire is not at right angles to the field, state that the force will be less than the maximum.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Permanent magnets always have a field; induced magnets are temporary and always attracted to the magnetising magnet.
  • A solenoid with an iron core makes an electromagnet. Its strength depends on current, number of turns and the core material. It can be switched on and off.
  • Motor effect: \(F = BIl\). Use Fleming’s left-hand rule (Thumb = Force, First = Field, Second = Current). A split-ring commutator keeps a motor spinning.

glossary_terms.definition: A magnet that produces its own magnetic field at all times.
A material that becomes temporarily magnetic when placed in a magnetic field.
The region around a magnet where a magnetic force acts.
A coil of wire that produces a strong magnetic field when current flows through it.
A solenoid with a soft iron core, creating a strong magnet that can be switched on and off.
Materials that are attracted to magnets and can be magnetised, including iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
The force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T).
A rule for finding force direction: thumb = force, first finger = field, second finger = current.
